news.title: [SMM News] Zambia Aims to Boost EV and Battery Production to Maximize Value from Critical MineralsZambia is seeking investment in battery and electric vehicle manufacturing to retain more value from its mineral resources. The latest investment appeal reinforces that ambition without announcing a plant capacity or commissioning schedule. Neighbouring Zimbabwe offers a regional example of progress in lithium processing, although concentrates still dominate its lithium export earnings. Zambia seeks investment across the battery and EV chain In a statement made on the 22nd of October 2026, the Zambia Development Agency (ZDA) had urged investment in EV, battery and component manufacturing near mineral sources. Speaking at the Zambia Mining Insaka CEO Roundtable, emphasis on predictable policy and which value-added products Zambia should export through the Lobito Corridor. The statement gives no committed investment value, plant capacity or start date. Lithium potential still requires commercial definition ZDA also highlighted lithium alongside nickel and manganese, which are major battery materials. Lithium was already included in Zambia’s National Critical Minerals Strategy 2024-2028. The strategy records occurrences around Mapatizya in Southern Province, Nyimba and Lundazi in Eastern Province, and several districts in Central Province. Occurrences alone do not establish commercially mineable reserves or a reliable supply of battery-grade feedstock. The ambition also builds on the Zambia–DRC battery initiative. UNECA reported in April 2024 that the countries were reviewing a pre-feasibility study for a joint battery and EV special economic zone, following a March 2023 framework agreement. Zimbabwe adds lithium sulphate to its export mix MMCZ figures put Zimbabwe’s lithium export sales at approximately US$2.159 billion in January-September 2026. Lithium sulphate contributed US$190.52 million on an estimated 33,807 mt, compared with no recorded sulphate sales in the corresponding period of 2025. Mining Zimbabwe attributed the sulphate exports to Huayou’s Arcadia operation. Huayou said its Zimbabwe base held its first lithium sulphate shipment ceremony on 25 April 2026. Its ATZ refinery is located beside the Prospect Lithium Zimbabwe (PLZ) concentrator in the Arcadia mining area and has a stated design capacity of 50,000 mt of lithium sulphate a year in product capacity. Zimbabwe lithium export sales in January-September 2026 Product Value US$ million Share of reported total Spodumene concentrate 1,812 83.9% Lithium sulphate 190.52 8.8% Petalite 155.29 7.2% Reported total ≈2,159 100% Zimbabwe’s government has maintained its stated plan to ban lithium concentrate exports from January 2027. A February 2026 suspension was followed by a resumption under export quotas. The pace of new processing capacity and any transition arrangements will be important for 2027 feedstock availability. Lithium sulphate is an intermediate product Lithium sulphate requires further conversion into lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide for battery materials. Component and cell manufacturing, followed by pack and vehicle assembly, involve additional processes and inputs. Spodumene assessments fell about 24 percent from 9 to 30 October The three Zimbabwean spodumene grades fell by 24.0-24.6% between early to late October 2026. All three declined in each of the three weekly comparisons. The 6% Li₂O assessment reached US$1,295/mt on 30 October, within a range of US$1,250-1,340/mt. SMM assessment values supplied in the draft. CIF Chinese main ports, dry basis. Historical values were not independently retrieved from the public pages; see the data note. Zimbabwean spodumene assessments in October 2026 Grade 9 Oct 16 Oct 23 Oct 30 Oct 30 Oct range 9-30 Oct change 6% Li₂O 1,705 1,480 1,405 1,295 1,250-1,340 -410 (-24.0%) 5.5% Li₂O 1,585 1,400 1,315 1,200 1,160-1,240 -385 (-24.3%) 5% Li₂O 1,485 1,320 1,225 1,120 1,030-1,210 -365 (-24.6%) US$/mt, dry basis; CIF Chinese main ports. Fe₂O₃ ≤1.5%, mica ≤3%, moisture ≤15%. Values and ranges are from the supplied draft; changes are recalculated. In the week to 30 October, the 6% grade fell US$110/mt (7.83%), the 5.5% grade fell US$115/mt (8.75%) and the 5% grade fell US$105/mt (8.57%). The largest absolute weekly decline occurred from 9 to 16 October, at US$225/mt, US$185/mt and US$165/mt, respectively. SMM view For Zambia, the next test is whether investment promotion produces projects with defined feedstock, financing, reliable power and customer offtake. Chemical processing, battery cell production and EV assembly need separate capacity targets and commissioning milestones. Zimbabwe’s experience demonstrates a route into intermediate chemicals; however, does not establish the economics of a Zambian battery or EV plant. Progress should be judged by disclosed resource assessments, financed plants, commissioned throughput and executed offtakes, with separate milestones for chemical processing, cell production and EV assembly.Nov 18, 2026 18:50 (GMT+8)

news.title: [SMM Analysis] Lithium Carbonate Market in Deficit in Q3 2026: Why Prices Failed to Rise？In Q3 2026, China's lithium carbonate market saw a weak trend with the price center moving lower month by month. Alongside the persistently weakening prices, the supply-demand balance was negative for three consecutive months. The deficit moving in the opposite direction of prices was the most noteworthy phenomenon of the quarter. Prices did not fall sharply in a one-way move, but instead declined stepwise on a monthly basis: a stalemate between upstream and downstream in July, narrow consolidation in August, and a marked acceleration of the decline in September, with month-end spot prices having pulled back nearly 40% from the year's high in mid-May. I. Price Path: From Two-Way Tug-of-War to One-Way Decline The market was in a stalemate in July. Downstream players bought the dip below the 150,000 yuan/mt level but showed little willingness to chase prices above 160,000 yuan/mt; upstream held quotes firm with limited room for concessions. The psychological price spread between the two sides persisted throughout the quarter, with transactions concentrated at the lower end of the price range and the average price pulling back slightly MoM. In August, some lithium chemical plants resumed production after maintenance, while upstream continued to hold prices firm and downstream maintained purchasing as needed. The phased mismatch was not resolved, and the market entered consolidation, with the MoM decline in the average price narrowing to within 2%. The pattern changed in September: production resumptions after maintenance drove output higher, transactions slowed rapidly after pre-holiday stockpiling ended, the driver of concentrated buying disappeared, and the one-way downward shift in the price center was confirmed, with the monthly decline widening notably. II. Supply: The Mismatch Between Maintenance and Production Resumptions The pace of supply in Q3 corresponded closely with the pace of prices. In July, some smelters on both the spodumene and lepidolite routes underwent concentrated maintenance, with production falling nearly 10% MoM, which became the main factor supporting prices. From August onward, production resumptions after maintenance proceeded one after another, salt lakes entered their seasonal peak production period, port arrivals of spodumene increased, and production rebounded MoM; September saw further slight growth. During the same period, production restrictions at salt lakes, maintenance shutdowns in the recycling segment, and raw material constraints on lithium extraction from slag utilization formed offsets, limiting the extent of the supply recovery—supply elasticity was restored, but growth did not get out of control. The implication of this pace is that the tightness in July was at the production schedule level, not the resource level. The market already had expectations for the production resumption timetable, so when production rebounded as scheduled in August and September, prices did not receive effective support. Instead, the realization of expectations removed the upside potential. III. Demand: The source of growth has shifted The demand side showed clear divergence across levels. Throughout the quarter, cathode material and battery cell production continued to grow QoQ, with cumulative growth in the battery cell segment exceeding 20%; NEV sales, however, declined MoM twice in July and September, with cumulative quarterly decline of nearly 10%. This means the growth in lithium demand in Q3 was no longer primarily driven by the vehicle segment. This structural shift in demand has direct implications for lithium carbonate: the cathode routes corresponding to energy storage and export orders are dominated by LFP, whose raw material is precisely lithium carbonate. This also provides a structural explanation for why the decline in lithium carbonate prices was smaller than what NEV sales would suggest—the center of demand is shifting from passenger vehicles to power-side energy storage projects. The divergence in demand also explains purchasing behavior. Cathode and battery cell enterprises maintained production amid moderate order visibility, but refused to build raw material inventory amid expectations of falling prices, creating a combination of "rising production, cautious purchasing." IV. Policy: Costs shift from implicit to explicit On July 17, three government departments issued a notice imposing a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries effective September 1, at a rate of 2%, rising to 4% from September 2027, covering production, commissioned processing, and import/export stages. Three details in the policy design determine its market impact: complete energy storage systems are tax-exempt; battery cells assembled into battery clusters are taxable but deductible; exports are taxed first and refunded later, with the refund rate reduced from 9% to 6%. The significance of the policy for Q3 market conditions lies not in the tax rate itself, but in the shift of the tax burden on battery cells and battery clusters from implicit to explicit. Explicit costs can be passed through; implicit costs can only be absorbed. In the short term, the implementation of the tax burden compressed profit margins in the battery cell and battery cluster segments, reinforcing downstream purchasing as needed and pushing for lower prices; the acceleration of the price decline in September coincided with the September 1 implementation date. In the medium term, the explicit tax burden will accelerate the exit of inefficient capacity, which directionally helps raise the cost curve, but this effect is not reflected in Q3 prices. Meanwhile, Shandong Document No. 632 removed the pre-approval constraint on grid connection for new wind and solar power projects with energy storage allocation, allowing enterprises to independently determine the scale, duration, and technology route of energy storage allocation. For operational PV and wind power projects included in the plan, the energy storage allocation caps are 50% and 30% of installed capacity, respectively, with unified dispatch, metering, settlement, and participation in the spot market. The shift from mandatory energy storage allocation to economic-driven deployment means short-term lithium demand growth depends more on spot revenue, weakening the floor effect. V. Inventory: The Extent and Structure of Destocking Inventory changes provide direct evidence of demand divergence. During the thirteen weeks from early July to early October, inventories across major segments fell by more than 30% in aggregate. The structural differences are even more noteworthy: downstream cathode plant inventories were nearly halved, smelter inventories fell by nearly 40%, while trader inventories pulled back only slightly, with their share of total inventory rising from under 30% to over one-third. The destocking was concentrated downstream, indicating that Q3 inventory changes were driven by the consumption side rather than proactive destocking on the production side. Upstream players completed shipments through long-term contract deliveries and holding back from selling, while cathode plants ran their raw material inventories down to relatively low levels. September purchases included some pre-holiday restocking at low prices, but trading quickly turned thin once stockpiling ended. The decline in absolute inventory levels and the shift in structure occurred simultaneously: as total volume decreased, inventory holdings tilted from industrial segments toward trading segments. The implications of this shift for prices differ from those of the change in total volume—industrial inventory will be consumed, whereas trading inventory tends to be released when prices rebound. The same quantity, held by different parties, does not act on prices in the same direction. VI. The Divergence Between Deficits and Prices The Q3 supply-demand balance was negative for three consecutive months, with a cumulative quarterly deficit of approximately 84,000 mt LCE; correspondingly, the price center moved lower month by month. The deficit and prices moving in opposite directions is key to understanding this quarter's market. The two can be reconciled in the data. Over the same period, inventory destocking amounted to approximately 68,000 mt, on the same order of magnitude as the quarterly deficit—the deficit was largely filled by inventory rather than cleared through prices. Inventory served as a buffer, allowing prices to continue falling despite the existence of a deficit. This is the first explanation for the coexistence of a deficit and falling prices. The second explanation lies in the time dimension of pricing. What the market traded in Q3 was not the spot tightness from July to September, but rather the supply recovery after production resumptions and expectations of more distant supply growth. news.summary: [SMM Analysis] Lithium Carbonate Market in Deficit in Q3 2026: Why Prices Failed to Rise？In Q3 2026, China's lithium carbonate market saw a weak trend with the price center moving lower month by month. Alongside the persistently weakening prices, the supply-demand balance was negative for three consecutive months. The deficit moving in the opposite direction of prices was the most noteworthy phenomenon of the quarter. Prices did not fall sharply in a one-way move, but instead declined stepwise on a monthly basis: a stalemate between upstream and downstream in July, narrow consolidation in August, and a marked acceleration of the decline in September, with month-end spot prices having pulled back nearly 40% from the year's high in mid-May. I. Price Path: From Two-Way Tug-of-War to One-Way Decline The market was in a stalemate in July. Downstream players bought the dip below the 150,000 yuan/mt level but showed little willingness to chase prices above 160,000 yuan/mt; upstream held quotes firm with limited room for concessions. The psychological price spread between the two sides persisted throughout the quarter, with transactions concentrated at the lower end of the price range and the average price pulling back slightly MoM. In August, some lithium chemical plants resumed production after maintenance, while upstream continued to hold prices firm and downstream maintained purchasing as needed. The phased mismatch was not resolved, and the market entered consolidation, with the MoM decline in the average price narrowing to within 2%. The pattern changed in September: production resumptions after maintenance drove output higher, transactions slowed rapidly after pre-holiday stockpiling ended, the driver of concentrated buying disappeared, and the one-way downward shift in the price center was confirmed, with the monthly decline widening notably. II. Supply: The Mismatch Between Maintenance and Production Resumptions The pace of supply in Q3 corresponded closely with the pace of prices. In July, some smelters on both the spodumene and lepidolite routes underwent concentrated maintenance, with production falling nearly 10% MoM, which became the main factor supporting prices. From August onward, production resumptions after maintenance proceeded one after another, salt lakes entered their seasonal peak production period, port arrivals of spodumene increased, and production rebounded MoM; September saw further slight growth. During the same period, production restrictions at salt lakes, maintenance shutdowns in the recycling segment, and raw material constraints on lithium extraction from slag utilization formed offsets, limiting the extent of the supply recovery—supply elasticity was restored, but growth did not get out of control. The implication of this pace is that the tightness in July was at the production schedule level, not the resource level. The market already had expectations for the production resumption timetable, so when production rebounded as scheduled in August and September, prices did not receive effective support. Instead, the realization of expectations removed the upside potential. III. Demand: The source of growth has shifted The demand side showed clear divergence across levels. Throughout the quarter, cathode material and battery cell production continued to grow QoQ, with cumulative growth in the battery cell segment exceeding 20%; NEV sales, however, declined MoM twice in July and September, with cumulative quarterly decline of nearly 10%. This also provides a structural explanation for why the decline in lithium carbonate prices was smaller than what NEV sales would suggest—the center of demand is shifting from passenger vehicles to power-side energy storage projects. The divergence in demand also explains purchasing behavior. Cathode and battery cell enterprises maintained production amid moderate order visibility, but refused to build raw material inventory amid expectations of falling prices, creating a combination of "rising production, cautious purchasing." The significance of the policy for Q3 market conditions lies not in the tax rate itself, but in the shift of the tax burden on battery cells and battery clusters from implicit to explicit. news.title: Lithium Market: From End-User Consumption and Active Destocking to the Mismatch in Marginal Procurement [SMM Analysis]1. Core Conclusions The key issue in the current lithium market is not a collapse in end demand, but rather that active destocking across the supply chain has amplified changes in end-user demand, leaving upstream producers facing marginal procurement demand that is significantly weaker than actual consumption. Over the past month, the inventory structure has changed materially: destocking has been concentrated mainly at the downstream level, while inventories held by lithium salt producers and other market participants have increased. This structure suggests that the current inventory drawdown should not simply be interpreted as evidence of strong spot procurement. On the contrary, downstream cathode material producers are meeting production needs by reducing raw material inventories, while remaining cautious on incremental spot purchases. Inventories are gradually shifting from consumption inventories toward producer-held and trading inventories. At the same time, cathode producers do not rely entirely on self-procured lithium salts. Some operate under customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements, whereby battery manufacturers, affiliated companies, or designated upstream suppliers provide lithium salts directly to cathode producers for processing. As a result, cathode output and cathode producers’ own lithium salt procurement are not necessarily correlated on a one-to-one basis. When the share of customer-supplied lithium salts rises, cathode production can remain elevated even without a corresponding increase in market-based spot procurement. The market can therefore experience tight supply-demand balances, declining inventories, and weak prices at the same time. The reason is that prices are primarily driven by marginal procurement rather than by end consumption itself. As long as the supply chain remains in an active destocking phase, and part of cathode production continues to be supported by long-term contracts and customer-supplied lithium salts, cathode and battery producers can maintain relatively high production levels while significantly reducing their purchases in the open market. A genuine price inflection point is more likely to emerge when the supply chain shifts from “destocking” to “stable inventories” or even “restocking.” At that point, normal production demand and inventory replenishment demand could be released simultaneously, creating procurement growth that is significantly stronger than the growth in end demand. 2. Total Inventories Are Still Falling, but Inventory Ownership Has Changed From an aggregate perspective, lithium carbonate inventories are still trending lower. However, the structure of this drawdown is notably different from a conventional demand-driven destocking cycle. The most significant feature is that downstream inventories have fallen sharply on a weekly basis, while inventories held by lithium salt producers and other market participants have increased. This indicates that inventory ownership is shifting away from downstream consumers toward lithium salt producers and trading intermediaries. Downstream cathode producers are increasingly operating with lean inventories rather than actively rebuilding raw material stocks during a falling-price environment. Lithium salt producers, meanwhile, have shown some reluctance to sell aggressively at low prices, while trading intermediaries are increasingly performing functions related to price positioning, title transfer, and tactical inventory management. A more accurate description of the current inventory trend is therefore that total inventories are still declining, but inventories are migrating from downstream consumers toward upstream suppliers and intermediate trading channels. This change is important for assessing price elasticity. Downstream inventories primarily serve as production buffer stocks and are relatively rigid, whereas inventories held by traders and lithium salt producers are more price-sensitive. If prices rebound, these latter inventories are more likely to return to the market as potential spot supply, thereby creating upside resistance. 3. Cathode Material Output Has Not Fallen in Parallel, Indicating a Decoupling Between “Consumption” and “Procurement” Cathode material production remains relatively high. According to SMM data, weekly LFP output is approximately 141,600 mt, while ternary cathode material output is around 18,000 mt. Ternary output has declined for nine consecutive weeks, but LFP production remains elevated. Assuming approximately 0.24 mt of lithium carbonate consumption per tonne of LFP, weekly theoretical lithium carbonate consumption associated with LFP production alone would be around 34,000 mt LCE, exceeding the total lithium carbonate inventory reported at cathode producers. This should not, however, be interpreted simply as meaning that downstream inventories are insufficient to support one week of production. First, visible SMM inventory does not capture all lithium salt resources available to cathode producers, which may also include in-transit material, long-term contract deliveries, and raw materials already in the production process. More importantly, customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements are relatively common in the cathode industry. Under such arrangements, part of the lithium salts consumed by cathode producers is not purchased directly by the cathode producer itself, but instead supplied by battery manufacturers, affiliated entities, or designated suppliers. Cathode producers’ visible inventories and self-procured volumes therefore cannot be treated as equivalent to their total lithium salt availability or actual consumption. A more reasonable interpretation is that visible downstream lithium carbonate inventories have been compressed to relatively low levels, but cathode producers can still maintain production through long-term contracts, customer-supplied lithium salts, and continuous deliveries. This is one of the most important current market features: cathode output has not declined materially, but cathode producers’ own procurement and willingness to purchase in the spot market have clearly weakened. After the pre-holiday restocking cycle ended in October, some cathode producers continued to reduce raw material inventories. Procurement appetite among ternary producers has been particularly weak due to continued production cuts, while LFP producers, despite maintaining high output, have also tended to purchase only on a just-in-time basis, relying more heavily on long-term contracts, customer-supplied lithium salts, and lean inventory management. The market therefore needs to distinguish clearly between “actual lithium salt consumption” and “cathode producers’ own procurement.” Especially when customer-supplied material accounts for a high share of input supply, elevated cathode production does not necessarily translate into stronger open-market buying. 4. Why Can Upstream Orders Weaken Sharply Even if End Demand Does Not? The key relationship is that procurement depends on actual consumption, inventory changes, and the share of customer-supplied material. For a producer relying entirely on self-procurement, procurement can be approximated as: Procurement = Actual Consumption + Change in Inventory For cathode producers that also receive customer-supplied lithium salts, the volume supplied by customers or affiliated parties must be deducted from their own market procurement. Therefore, when cathode producers actively destock while the share of customer-supplied material rises, their market-based procurement can fall well below actual production consumption. For example, assume a cathode producer consumes 100 units of lithium salts per week. If inventories are stable and all material is self-procured, procurement would be approximately 100 units. If the producer actively reduces inventories by 20 units, procurement may fall to 80 units. If a further 20 units are supplied by a customer, the cathode producer’s own open-market procurement may decline to just 60 units. This illustrates that upstream suppliers can experience a sharp contraction in visible buying even if actual production demand is unchanged. This explains why the market can simultaneously observe stable end demand and weak lithium salt buying. The underlying reason is that inventory cycles and supply arrangements jointly amplify changes in end demand. Small changes in end-user demand are transmitted upstream through the supply chain: automakers reduce inventories, battery producers shorten inventory cycles, cathode producers reduce raw material stocks, and long-term contracts and customer-supplied lithium salts further reduce open-market procurement. As a result, lithium salt producers see much weaker effective buying than would be implied by actual end consumption. The weakness in the current lithium market should therefore not simply be attributed to collapsing end demand. A more accurate interpretation is that end consumption and upstream marginal procurement have decoupled, with active destocking and customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements jointly suppressing cathode producers’ demand in the open market. 5. Every Segment of the Supply Chain Is Doing the Same Thing: Reducing Inventory Risk Although the reasons differ across the supply chain, the direction of behavior is broadly the same: reducing inventory exposure. Automakers are relying more heavily on exports to absorb production while controlling domestic channel inventories. Battery producers are shortening inventory cycles and reducing finished cell and raw material stocks. Energy storage project developers, facing mismatches between project construction, grid connection, and delivery schedules, are delaying some product take-up. Cathode producers are reluctant to restock during a falling-price environment and prefer to rely on long-term contracts, customer-supplied lithium salts, and just-in-time procurement. Lithium salt producers are less willing to sell aggressively at prices approaching the cost levels of some higher-cost producers, while trading intermediaries are increasingly shifting from pure distribution toward price positioning and inventory management. Each of these decisions is rational in isolation, but when the entire supply chain reduces inventories simultaneously, the result is a significant reinforcing effect. At the cathode level in particular, active destocking reduces procurement demand, while customer-supplied lithium salts further reduce dependence on the spot market. As a result, the buying seen by upstream producers is materially weaker than actual end consumption. Current prices therefore reflect not only expectations for end demand, but also lower risk appetite and changes in procurement behavior across the broader supply chain. 6. The Mining Segment Is Operating on a Different Timeline: High Imports, High Port Inventories, and Falling Lithium Salt Inventories Can Coexist The upstream mining segment and the lithium salt market currently display very different inventory conditions. China imported approximately 970,100 physical tonnes of spodumene in September, up 7% month on month, including around 136,000 tonnes from Zimbabwe, up 83% month on month. At the same time, domestic port inventories of spodumene remain relatively high, while lithium carbonate inventories continue to decline. These two trends are not contradictory. Between lithium concentrate imports and the eventual production of lithium carbonate, material must pass through several stages, including port arrival, port storage, collection, refinery raw material inventories, feed preparation, conversion, and finished lithium carbonate inventory. This process creates a lag of several weeks to several months. More importantly, when lithium salt prices fall to or below the conversion cost of some externally sourced concentrate producers, or even some lithium residue processors, refinery margins become compressed. Under these conditions, refiners may reduce the pace of port withdrawals, cut spot concentrate purchases, lower operating rates, or defer conversion of certain feedstocks. It is therefore entirely possible for spodumene inventories at ports to remain high while lithium carbonate inventories continue to fall. This means mining supply cannot be assessed using a simple equation of “higher imports = higher lithium salt supply.” The more relevant variables are port inventories, withdrawal rates, refinery margins, and actual operating rates. Among these, refinery margins and withdrawal rates are particularly important because they determine when port-side concentrate inventories are actually converted into lithium salt supply. 7. Why Can Tightness, Destocking, and Weak Prices Exist at the Same Time? The market currently exhibits what appears to be a contradictory combination: relatively tight supply-demand balances, declining inventories, and weak prices. The key reason is that three variables operating across different time horizons are moving simultaneously. First, actual consumption can still exceed incremental supply, which leads to continued inventory drawdowns. Second, downstream participants can actively reduce inventories and increase their reliance on long-term contracts and customer-supplied material, causing self-procurement to remain below actual consumption. Third, the market can price in future supply improvements or slower demand growth in advance, placing pressure on prices. Inventory drawdowns therefore reflect current supply-demand conditions, procurement reflects inventory strategy and supply structure, while prices reflect expected future marginal changes. These three factors do not need to move in lockstep. This also explains why looking only at total market inventories can easily overstate demand strength. The key question is where inventories are declining and who is absorbing them. If inventories are mainly falling at cathode producers while increasing at lithium salt producers and traders, the bullish implication is much weaker than in a scenario where producer inventories are falling and downstream inventories are rising due to active restocking. 8. Three “Gaps” Will Determine When Prices Regain Upside Momentum There are currently three key mismatches across the supply chain that warrant close monitoring. The first is the gap between vehicle production and wholesale volumes on one side, and retail demand on the other. Automakers can absorb production through exports, dealer inventories, and promotions, but as long as retail demand remains insufficient, they will retain an incentive to reduce inventories. The second is the gap between energy storage battery shipments and actual project grid connection. Storage cell shipments do not immediately translate into effective end consumption, as delays can arise from project construction, grid connection, commissioning, and delivery schedules. The third is the gap between cathode material output and market-based lithium salt procurement, which is currently the most directly relevant mismatch for lithium prices. Cathode producers can maintain procurement below theoretical lithium salt consumption by reducing inventories, while customer-supplied lithium salts can further lower their own procurement needs. However, both mechanisms have limits. Inventories cannot be reduced indefinitely, and customer-supplied material merely transfers the identity of the buyer rather than eliminating actual lithium salt consumption. Once raw material inventories approach minimum operating levels and customer-supplied counterparties begin to face their own inventory or procurement constraints, overall supply-chain buying must eventually return to the market. 9. A Genuine Price Reversal Could Be Driven by the Combination of “Production Demand + Restocking Demand” During a destocking phase, market-based procurement remains below actual production demand. When inventories stabilize, procurement gradually converges toward actual consumption. During a restocking phase, procurement can exceed actual production demand. When customer-supplied lithium salts are included, the market must monitor not only a recovery in cathode producers’ own procurement, but also whether the suppliers providing customer-owned material increase their own purchases. Customer-supplied arrangements do not alter final lithium salt consumption; they simply change who is purchasing material in the market. For example, if actual cathode consumption is 100 units, cathode producers may procure only 80 units during a destocking phase. If 20 units are additionally supplied by customers, the cathode producer’s open-market procurement may fall to 60 units. Later, if actual demand rises to 105 units and the supply chain needs to rebuild 20 units of inventory, total supply-chain procurement can increase sharply even if the share of customer-supplied material remains unchanged. This means end demand only needs to improve modestly for procurement growth to be much stronger. The key issue going forward is therefore not whether individual cathode producers increase purchases, but whether lithium salt procurement across the entire supply chain shifts from “distributed customer supply + destocking” toward “active inventory rebuilding.” If several of these inventory gaps begin narrowing around the first quarter of 2027, the lithium salt market could simultaneously receive demand from production recovery and inventory replenishment, thereby amplifying price elasticity. 10. Five Leading Indicators to Monitor The first indicator should be market-based procurement intensity at the cathode level. A simple ratio of “cathode producer procurement / cathode production” can be distorted by changes in the share of customer-supplied lithium salts. A better framework would therefore separate cathode producers’ own procurement, long-term contract deliveries, and customer-supplied lithium salts, and then track self-procurement as a share of actual lithium salt consumption. If cathode production remains stable while both self-procurement and total supply-chain procurement begin to rise, this would be a stronger signal that active destocking is nearing an end. The second indicator is downstream inventory days. Absolute inventory tonnage is less informative than the number of production days covered by those inventories. Inventory coverage should also be assessed alongside long-term contracts, customer-supplied material, and in-transit cargoes to estimate the true minimum operating inventory level. The third indicator is inventory ownership. The key metrics should include the inventory shares held by downstream consumers, lithium salt producers, and traders or other intermediaries. If downstream inventory shares begin to recover while trader inventories decline, this would be more consistent with genuine restocking. The fourth indicator is conversion margins for externally sourced spodumene. Refinery profitability determines when port-side concentrate is likely to be converted into lithium salt supply. If conversion margins remain negative, high port inventories may not translate quickly into higher lithium salt production. The fifth indicator is the combination of basis, warehouse receipts, and spot-market structure. A credible improvement in fundamentals should be accompanied by stronger spot transactions, increased purchasing by cathode producers and customer-supply counterparties, stronger basis, declining warehouse receipts, and stabilization of downstream inventories. If futures prices rise while neither cathode producers nor customer-supply counterparties increase purchases, the rally is more likely to reflect expectations and trading flows rather than a genuine improvement in physical demand. 11. Price Triggers and Validation Framework Three categories of signals should be monitored closely. First, cathode producers’ own procurement and total supply-chain procurement should begin to rise relative to cathode production, which would provide the clearest indication that the inventory cycle is approaching a bottom. Second, the share of inventories held by traders and other intermediaries should decline while downstream inventories stabilize, indicating that inventories are moving back from trading channels into consumption inventories. Third, port-side concentrate pressure should ease, or production cuts among high-cost lithium refiners should materialize, reducing future lithium salt supply pressure. If prices rebound while cathode producers’ own procurement remains weak and customer-supply counterparties also fail to increase market purchases, the underlying weakness is more likely to reflect genuine demand softness rather than a pure inventory-cycle effect. Conversely, if prices remain weak but both cathode producers’ own procurement and customer-supply purchases recover, trader inventories stop rising, and refinery production cuts materialize, the physical market may already be forming a bottom even before prices fully reflect that shift. 12. Conclusion The most important issue in the current lithium market is not simply the size of the supply-demand gap or the fact that inventories are declining, but rather the mismatch between inventory structure, procurement behavior, customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements, and end consumption. At present, actual end consumption has not fallen by as much as upstream procurement. Weak prices are increasingly driven by active destocking and changes in the identity of the buyer. Automakers are controlling channel inventories, battery producers are shortening inventory cycles, cathode producers are reducing raw material inventories and lowering their own spot procurement through long-term contracts and customer-supplied lithium salts, some energy storage deliveries are being deferred, lithium salt producers are less willing to sell aggressively at low prices, and trading inventories are increasing. Together, these factors have made upstream marginal buying significantly weaker than actual end consumption. At the same time, inventories are migrating from downstream consumption inventories toward lithium salt producers and trading inventories. As a result, falling total inventories should not automatically be interpreted as stronger demand. From a price-transmission perspective, the key question is not whether end demand suddenly accelerates, but when the supply chain completes its active destocking cycle and lithium salt buyers begin rebuilding inventories. Once cathode inventories approach minimum operating levels, participants shift from “destocking” to “stable inventories” or “restocking,” and customer-supply counterparties also increase their own procurement, normal production demand and inventory replenishment demand could combine to generate upstream order growth well above the pace of end-demand growth. The core market thesis can therefore be summarized as follows: Lithium prices are driven by marginal procurement rather than by end consumption itself. Current weakness reflects the combined impact of the inventory cycle and customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements, while the next price inflection point will depend on when the supply-chain inventory cycle turns positive and when purchasing activity returns to the open market. After the pre-holiday restocking cycle ended in October, some cathode producers continued to reduce raw material inventories. Procurement appetite among ternary producers has been particularly weak due to continued production cuts, while LFP producers, despite maintaining high output, have also tended to purchase only on a just-in-time basis, relying more heavily on long-term contracts, customer-supplied lithium salts, and lean inventory management. The market therefore needs to distinguish clearly between “actual lithium salt consumption” and “cathode producers’ own procurement.” Especially when customer-supplied material accounts for a high share of input supply, elevated cathode production does not necessarily translate into stronger open-market buying. 4. Why Can Upstream Orders Weaken Sharply Even if End Demand Does Not? The key relationship is that procurement depends on actual consumption, inventory changes, and the share of customer-supplied material. For a producer relying entirely on self-procurement, procurement can be approximated as: Procurement = Actual Consumption + Change in Inventory For cathode producers that also receive customer-supplied lithium salts, the volume supplied by customers or affiliated parties must be deducted from their own market procurement. Therefore, when cathode producers actively destock while the share of customer-supplied material rises, their market-based procurement can fall well below actual production consumption. For example, assume a cathode producer consumes 100 units of lithium salts per week. If inventories are stable and all material is self-procured, procurement would be approximately 100 units. If the producer actively reduces inventories by 20 units, procurement may fall to 80 units. If a further 20 units are supplied by a customer, the cathode producer’s own open-market procurement may decline to just 60 units. This illustrates that upstream suppliers can experience a sharp contraction in visible buying even if actual production demand is unchanged. This explains why the market can simultaneously observe stable end demand and weak lithium salt buying. The underlying reason is that inventory cycles and supply arrangements jointly amplify changes in end demand. Small changes in end-user demand are transmitted upstream through the supply chain: automakers reduce inventories, battery producers shorten inventory cycles, cathode producers reduce raw material stocks, and long-term contracts and customer-supplied lithium salts further reduce open-market procurement. As a result, lithium salt producers see much weaker effective buying than would be implied by actual end consumption. The weakness in the current lithium market should therefore not simply be attributed to collapsing end demand. A more accurate interpretation is that end consumption and upstream marginal procurement have decoupled, with active destocking and customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements jointly suppressing cathode producers’ demand in the open market. 5. Every Segment of the Supply Chain Is Doing the Same Thing: Reducing Inventory Risk Although the reasons differ across the supply chain, the direction of behavior is broadly the same: reducing inventory exposure. Automakers are relying more heavily on exports to absorb production while controlling domestic channel inventories. Battery producers are shortening inventory cycles and reducing finished cell and raw material stocks. Energy storage project developers, facing mismatches between project construction, grid connection, and delivery schedules, are delaying some product take-up. Cathode producers are reluctant to restock during a falling-price environment and prefer to rely on long-term contracts, customer-supplied lithium salts, and just-in-time procurement. Lithium salt producers are less willing to sell aggressively at prices approaching the cost levels of some higher-cost producers, while trading intermediaries are increasingly shifting from pure distribution toward price positioning and inventory management. Each of these decisions is rational in isolation, but when the entire supply chain reduces inventories simultaneously, the result is a significant reinforcing effect. At the cathode level in particular, active destocking reduces procurement demand, while customer-supplied lithium salts further reduce dependence on the spot market. As a result, the buying seen by upstream producers is materially weaker than actual end consumption. Current prices therefore reflect not only expectations for end demand, but also lower risk appetite and changes in procurement behavior across the broader supply chain. 6. The Mining Segment Is Operating on a Different Timeline: High Imports, High Port Inventories, and Falling Lithium Salt Inventories Can Coexist The upstream mining segment and the lithium salt market currently display very different inventory conditions. China imported approximately 970,100 physical tonnes of spodumene in September, up 7% month on month, including around 136,000 tonnes from Zimbabwe, up 83% month on month. At the same time, domestic port inventories of spodumene remain relatively high, while lithium carbonate inventories continue to decline. These two trends are not contradictory. Between lithium concentrate imports and the eventual production of lithium carbonate, material must pass through several stages, including port arrival, port storage, collection, refinery raw material inventories, feed preparation, conversion, and finished lithium carbonate inventory. This process creates a lag of several weeks to several months. More importantly, when lithium salt prices fall to or below the conversion cost of some externally sourced concentrate producers, or even some lithium residue processors, refinery margins become compressed. Under these conditions, refiners may reduce the pace of port withdrawals, cut spot concentrate purchases, lower operating rates, or defer conversion of certain feedstocks. It is therefore entirely possible for spodumene inventories at ports to remain high while lithium carbonate inventories continue to fall. This means mining supply cannot be assessed using a simple equation of “higher imports = higher lithium salt supply.” The more relevant variables are port inventories, withdrawal rates, refinery margins, and actual operating rates. Among these, refinery margins and withdrawal rates are particularly important because they determine when port-side concentrate inventories are actually converted into lithium salt supply. 7. Why Can Tightness, Destocking, and Weak Prices Exist at the Same Time? The market currently exhibits what appears to be a contradictory combination: relatively tight supply-demand balances, declining inventories, and weak prices. The key reason is that three variables operating across different time horizons are moving simultaneously. First, actual consumption can still exceed incremental supply, which leads to continued inventory drawdowns. Second, downstream participants can actively reduce inventories and increase their reliance on long-term contracts and customer-supplied material, causing self-procurement to remain below actual consumption. Third, the market can price in future supply improvements or slower demand growth in advance, placing pressure on prices. Inventory drawdowns therefore reflect current supply-demand conditions, procurement reflects inventory strategy and supply structure, while prices reflect expected future marginal changes. These three factors do not need to move in lockstep. This also explains why looking only at total market inventories can easily overstate demand strength. The key question is where inventories are declining and who is absorbing them. If inventories are mainly falling at cathode producers while increasing at lithium salt producers and traders, the bullish implication is much weaker than in a scenario where producer inventories are falling and downstream inventories are rising due to active restocking. 8. Three “Gaps” Will Determine When Prices Regain Upside Momentum There are currently three key mismatches across the supply chain that warrant close monitoring. The first is the gap between vehicle production and wholesale volumes on one side, and retail demand on the other. Automakers can absorb production through exports, dealer inventories, and promotions, but as long as retail demand remains insufficient, they will retain an incentive to reduce inventories. The second is the gap between energy storage battery shipments and actual project grid connection. Storage cell shipments do not immediately translate into effective end consumption, as delays can arise from project construction, grid connection, commissioning, and delivery schedules. The third is the gap between cathode material output and market-based lithium salt procurement, which is currently the most directly relevant mismatch for lithium prices. Cathode producers can maintain procurement below theoretical lithium salt consumption by reducing inventories, while customer-supplied lithium salts can further lower their own procurement needs. However, both mechanisms have limits. Inventories cannot be reduced indefinitely, and customer-supplied material merely transfers the identity of the buyer rather than eliminating actual lithium salt consumption. Once raw material inventories approach minimum operating levels and customer-supplied counterparties begin to face their own inventory or procurement constraints, overall supply-chain buying must eventually return to the market. 9. A Genuine Price Reversal Could Be Driven by the Combination of “Production Demand + Restocking Demand” During a destocking phase, market-based procurement remains below actual production demand. When inventories stabilize, procurement gradually converges toward actual consumption. During a restocking phase, procurement can exceed actual production demand. When customer-supplied lithium salts are included, the market must monitor not only a recovery in cathode producers’ own procurement, but also whether the suppliers providing customer-owned material increase their own purchases. Customer-supplied arrangements do not alter final lithium salt consumption; they simply change who is purchasing material in the market. For example, if actual cathode consumption is 100 units, cathode producers may procure only 80 units during a destocking phase. If 20 units are additionally supplied by customers, the cathode producer’s open-market procurement may fall to 60 units. Later, if actual demand rises to 105 units and the supply chain needs to rebuild 20 units of inventory, total supply-chain procurement can increase sharply even if the share of customer-supplied material remains unchanged. This means end demand only needs to improve modestly for procurement growth to be much stronger. The key issue going forward is therefore not whether individual cathode producers increase purchases, but whether lithium salt procurement across the entire supply chain shifts from “distributed customer supply + destocking” toward “active inventory rebuilding.” If several of these inventory gaps begin narrowing around the first quarter of 2027, the lithium salt market could simultaneously receive demand from production recovery and inventory replenishment, thereby amplifying price elasticity. 10. Five Leading Indicators to Monitor The first indicator should be market-based procurement intensity at the cathode level. A simple ratio of “cathode producer procurement / cathode production” can be distorted by changes in the share of customer-supplied lithium salts. A better framework would therefore separate cathode producers’ own procurement, long-term contract deliveries, and customer-supplied lithium salts, and then track self-procurement as a share of actual lithium salt consumption. If cathode production remains stable while both self-procurement and total supply-chain procurement begin to rise, this would be a stronger signal that active destocking is nearing an end. The second indicator is downstream inventory days. Absolute inventory tonnage is less informative than the number of production days covered by those inventories. Inventory coverage should also be assessed alongside long-term contracts, customer-supplied material, and in-transit cargoes to estimate the true minimum operating inventory level. The third indicator is inventory ownership. The key metrics should include the inventory shares held by downstream consumers, lithium salt producers, and traders or other intermediaries. If downstream inventory shares begin to recover while trader inventories decline, this would be more consistent with genuine restocking. The fourth indicator is conversion margins for externally sourced spodumene. Refinery profitability determines when port-side concentrate is likely to be converted into lithium salt supply. If conversion margins remain negative, high port inventories may not translate quickly into higher lithium salt production. The fifth indicator is the combination of basis, warehouse receipts, and spot-market structure. A credible improvement in fundamentals should be accompanied by stronger spot transactions, increased purchasing by cathode producers and customer-supply counterparties, stronger basis, declining warehouse receipts, and stabilization of downstream inventories. If futures prices rise while neither cathode producers nor customer-supply counterparties increase purchases, the rally is more likely to reflect expectations and trading flows rather than a genuine improvement in physical demand. 11. Price Triggers and Validation Framework Three categories of signals should be monitored closely. First, cathode producers’ own procurement and total supply-chain procurement should begin to rise relative to cathode production, which would provide the clearest indication that the inventory cycle is approaching a bottom. Second, the share of inventories held by traders and other intermediaries should decline while downstream inventories stabilize, indicating that inventories are moving back from trading channels into consumption inventories. Third, port-side concentrate pressure should ease, or production cuts among high-cost lithium refiners should materialize, reducing future lithium salt supply pressure. If prices rebound while cathode producers’ own procurement remains weak and customer-supply counterparties also fail to increase market purchases, the underlying weakness is more likely to reflect genuine demand softness rather than a pure inventory-cycle effect. Conversely, if prices remain weak but both cathode producers’ own procurement and customer-supply purchases recover, trader inventories stop rising, and refinery production cuts materialize, the physical market may already be forming a bottom even before prices fully reflect that shift. 12. Conclusion The most important issue in the current lithium market is not simply the size of the supply-demand gap or the fact that inventories are declining, but rather the mismatch between inventory structure, procurement behavior, customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements, and end consumption. At present, actual end consumption has not fallen by as much as upstream procurement. Weak prices are increasingly driven by active destocking and changes in the identity of the buyer. Automakers are controlling channel inventories, battery producers are shortening inventory cycles, cathode producers are reducing raw material inventories and lowering their own spot procurement through long-term contracts and customer-supplied lithium salts, some energy storage deliveries are being deferred, lithium salt producers are less willing to sell aggressively at low prices, and trading inventories are increasing. Together, these factors have made upstream marginal buying significantly weaker than actual end consumption. At the same time, inventories are migrating from downstream consumption inventories toward lithium salt producers and trading inventories. As a result, falling total inventories should not automatically be interpreted as stronger demand. From a price-transmission perspective, the key question is not whether end demand suddenly accelerates, but when the supply chain completes its active destocking cycle and lithium salt buyers begin rebuilding inventories. Once cathode inventories approach minimum operating levels, participants shift from “destocking” to “stable inventories” or “restocking,” and customer-supply counterparties also increase their own procurement, normal production demand and inventory replenishment demand could combine to generate upstream order growth well above the pace of end-demand growth. The core market thesis can therefore be summarized as follows: Lithium prices are driven by marginal procurement rather than by end consumption itself. Current weakness reflects the combined impact of the inventory cycle and customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements, while the next price inflection point will depend on when the supply-chain inventory cycle turns positive and when purchasing activity returns to the open market. news.title: Global Electronics Industry Faces PCB Shortage, Impacting Multiple Sectors Until 2028The global electronics industry is facing a severe shortage of printed circuit boards (PCBs). The US-based global electronics association warned in an alert report that these parts are found in nearly all consumer products containing electronic components, and the supply deficit could have a broad impact on the global economy. Currently, many enterprises in the automotive, medical, national defense, aerospace and other industries are already experiencing supply delays or are preparing for delivery setbacks that could last weeks or even months.The bottleneck lies upstream rather than in finished products. The association noted that demand has exceeded supply capability at every link of the supply chain, from fiberglass cloth and resin to finished circuit boards. Although manufacturing capacity is expanding, especially in Asia, what truly constrains supply are the upstream links, including fiberglass, resin, copper foil and production equipment. The organization judges that the supply bottleneck will persist at least until H1 2027, and substantial relief is unlikely before mid-2028.10 hours ago
